Turf ribbons between Southchase's paver driveways

Turf set between pavers in Southchase, a driveway ribbon, a stepping-stone path or an edging strip, is quoted per job rather than a flat per-foot rate, since the layout and how much cutting a curved paver pattern needs both change the labor. Paver driveways and walkways are common across Southchase's 1990s and early-2000s subdivisions, and a turf strip between them beats bare sand or a gravel fill that migrates.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Paver driveways are common across Southchase's older subdivisions

A share of Southchase's homes, built through the 1990s and into the early 2000s, use paver driveways and walkways rather than plain poured concrete, a detail found in several of the community's neighborhood real-estate profiles alongside its stucco-and-arch architectural style. Wherever pavers meet a planting bed or a driveway edge, a thin strip of exposed sand or crushed base is common, and that strip is exactly what turf ribbons are built to replace.

One grade, two base materials under a Southchase ribbon

Pavers want a dense-graded aggregate compacted tight enough to carry a tire's point load, while the turf beside them needs the opposite: a washed, open-graded crushed rock or crushed concrete layer that lets water pass straight through instead of locking together. On a Southchase paver-and-turf job the two materials meet at a single finished grade set before either one goes down, so the strip doesn't sit proud of or sunk below the hardscape once both are compacted. Keeping the layout continuous while letting the base underneath change at the joint is what makes the two materials behave as one surface instead of two competing ones.

Why turf beats loose rock between pavers on flatwoods sand

Loose gravel or shell fill between pavers migrates into the joints and onto the driveway itself after a Southchase wet season, and bare sand in that same strip washes out during a heavy summer storm. A narrow turf ribbon, bonded to a compacted base the same way a full lawn is, stays put through both problems and gives the strip a finished edge without adding a mowing task to a space too narrow for a mower anyway.

Why a checkerboard patio uses one product across every square

A checkerboard patio alternating paver squares with turf squares reads as one design, so the turf inside every square on a Southchase patio needs to be the same product, same pile height, same infill, rather than whatever was left over from other jobs. Mixing products across squares shows up quickly as some squares fading or wearing at a different rate than the rest, since even turf built to last ten to twenty years ages differently depending on stabilization and infill. Ordering enough of one product to cover every square from the start avoids a patchwork look setting in within the first few seasons.

Say you have a paver walkway in Parcel 6

Say you have a paver walkway in Parcel 6 running from the driveway to the front door, with an 18-inch-wide strip of bare, weedy sand on either side, about 120 sq ft combined. A turf ribbon along both sides of that walkway replaces the bare strip with a finished edge and stops weeds from pushing up between the paver joints from the side. Because the job is mostly cutting turf to a narrow, curved shape rather than covering open ground, pricing comes from a measured site visit rather than the same per-square-foot number a wide-open lawn would use.

Compacting the whole footprint before it splits into two bases

We grade and compact the full paver-and-turf footprint as one continuous surface before drawing the line between the dense-graded paver zone and the washed, open-graded turf zone, so both materials share the same finished elevation from the start. Splitting the footprint into its two base types too early, before the overall grade is settled, is how a Southchase project ends up with a paver course sitting slightly proud of or below the turf strip once everything is compacted in place. This sequencing step happens before either aggregate is ordered, since it decides how much of each material the job actually needs.

Assuming a mixed-material path near water is exempt because of the pavers

The state's ten-foot waterbody setback applies to turf specifically, not to pavers, so a Southchase path or patio mixing both materials near a pond or canal can't assume the whole layout is exempt just because part of it is hardscape. A design that treats the pavers as covering the setback question for the entire footprint risks having its turf sections flagged during review, or built too close and pulled back later, since the rule tracks where the turf itself sits regardless of what material runs alongside it.

Matching what a Southchase HOA already expects at the curb

Because paver driveways are already the norm in several Southchase phases, a turf ribbon between them tends to read as consistent with the street rather than as a change that draws HOA attention, though the specific phase association covering that address still sets its own review process for any exterior work. A sample swatch and a simple sketch showing where the ribbon runs is usually enough for that conversation.

Keeping a septic lid clear along a path that gets brushed regularly

Routine brushing and infill top-ups along a Southchase paver-and-turf walkway can gradually work material toward a septic lid near the path, covering it a little more with each pass unless someone deliberately checks that spot separately. Keeping the lid visibly clear, rather than assuming it'll turn up when it's needed, saves a search or a partial excavation the day a pump-out truck actually arrives. This is a small addition to a normal care routine, worth a specific look rather than an assumption that general upkeep handles it.

Questions people ask

Do most Southchase homes have paver or concrete driveways?

Paver driveways and walkways are common across several of Southchase's 1990s and early-2000s subdivisions, based on the community's own real-estate profiles, though concrete drives exist too depending on the phase and builder.

Does a narrow turf ribbon between pavers need its own base?

Yes, the same compacted, washed-rock base a full lawn needs, just built in a narrower trench sized to the strip between the pavers and the bed or driveway edge.
